clue.text: Turn into a flat European legume

indicators.note: into places the turn letter inside the run made by the flat and the European

parts.note: a fen is flat marshy land, as in the Fens of eastern England
a Greek is a European
U as in a U-turn

explanation.surface: Someone transforms into a flat European bean.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Turn' is U, as in U-turn, and 'into' puts it between FEN and GREEK.
explanation.definitionFit: Fenugreek is a plant of the pea family whose seeds are used as a spice, so it is a legume.

clue.text: Starve oneself, conserving energy, then eat well

indicators.note: conserving means holding on to, so the fasting word keeps the energy letter within it

parts.note: to fast is to go without food
E is the physics symbol for energy

explanation.surface: A dieter fasts to save energy, then gorges.
explanation.walkthrough: 'conserving' puts E inside FAST.
explanation.definitionFit: To feast is to dine lavishly, a banquet-style meal.

clue.text: Memories of a lasting love, perhaps?

indicators.note: perhaps suggests the letters might be arranged another way

parts.note: love is nil in tennis, the letter O

explanation.surface: Recollections of an enduring romance.
explanation.walkthrough: 'perhaps' rearranges A LASTING plus O (love, a zero score in tennis).
explanation.definitionFit: Nostalgia is a wistful longing for the past, a matter of fond recollection.

clue.text: Aim over the bar placed over poles, and he won't be needed!

definitions.text: Aim over the bar placed over poles, and he won't be needed!

parts.words: Aim over the bar placed over poles, and he won't be needed!
parts.note: the target is the frame of a crossbar on two posts; a shot sent over that bar needs no one to save it

explanation.surface: A footballer blasts the ball over the crossbar.
explanation.walkthrough: The aim is a goal (a bar placed over poles); when a shot flies over the bar, the player guarding it has nothing to do.
explanation.definitionFit: The player who guards the net is not needed when the shot misses the target entirely.

clue.text: Wear out pipe

definitions.meaning: the tube carrying fumes from an engine

explanation.definitionFit: To exhaust is to tire utterly; an exhaust is a car's tailpipe.

clue.text: Type of penguin allowed to be a warbler

parts.note: the king penguin is a species
let means permitted

explanation.surface: A penguin species is permitted to count as a songbird.
explanation.definitionFit: Kinglets are tiny songbirds such as the goldcrest, long grouped with the Old World warblers.

clue.text: Pulse found in steaming broth

indicators.note: steaming suggests the word broth bubbling and being stirred up

explanation.surface: A pulse such as a lentil turns up in a steaming broth.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pulse' looks like a lentil in the soup, but it is a heartbeat; 'steaming' rearranges BROTH.
explanation.definitionFit: A throb is a rhythmic beat, like a heartbeat.

clue.text: Food in a jam, but no starter

indicators.note: no starter means the first letter of the stuck word is dropped

parts.note: stuck means in a difficult position

explanation.surface: Food in a jar of jam, but no first course.
explanation.walkthrough: 'no starter' drops the S from STUCK. TUCK is British school slang for food, as in a tuck shop.
explanation.definitionFit: Tuck is slang for snacks and sweets, especially at school.

clue.text: Arm knocks top off pudding

indicators.note: knocks top off says the pudding word loses its first letter, as this is a down entry

parts.note: a trifle is a layered dessert of sponge, custard and cream

explanation.surface: Someone's arm knocks the top off a dessert.
explanation.walkthrough: 'knocks top off' removes T from TRIFLE, a British layered dessert.
explanation.definitionFit: A rifle is a firearm, and arms are weapons.

clue.text: Be cheesed off having begged

indicators.note: off suggests the letters have gone bad and are out of order

explanation.surface: Someone is fed up after pleading.
explanation.walkthrough: 'off' rearranges BE CHEESED; 'cheesed off' is British slang for annoyed.
explanation.definitionFit: To beseech is to implore, so beseeched means pleaded.

clue.text: Heading for Asia, east perhaps, in a boat

indicators.note: the heading of a word is its first letter, here of Asia
perhaps suggests the word east could be rearranged

explanation.surface: A ship sails eastward, bound for Asia.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Heading for' takes the A of Asia; 'perhaps' rearranges EAST into TSEA.
explanation.definitionFit: To be at sea is to be on the ocean, aboard ship.

clue.text: Irons, and one's dealt with parts of a shirt

parts.note: in card games the cards one is dealt form a hand
cuffs are the ends of a shirt's sleeves

explanation.surface: Someone irons the cuffs of a shirt after dealing with it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Irons' looks like the laundry verb, but it is the noun for shackles.
explanation.definitionFit: Irons are fetters or manacles placed on a prisoner's wrists.

clue.text: Bats all hunky, and FT too, I'm relieved to say

indicators.note: bats means crazy, so these letters go mad; it is also the setter's name

explanation.surface: The setter Bats is pleased that the FT is so handsome too.
explanation.walkthrough: Bats is the setter, but 'bats' (crazy) rearranges ALL HUNKY and FT.
explanation.definitionFit: The adverb expresses gratitude or relief at an outcome.

clue.text: It's in the report in the FT

indicators.note: in shows the letters sit inside the words the report

explanation.surface: It's covered in the paper's report.
explanation.walkthrough: The letters run across 'tHE REport'; 'in the FT' means in this newspaper, the place you are reading now.
explanation.definitionFit: Read in the FT itself, the paper is this very place.

clue.text: Puzzle: this should be grip ping, as set for the afternoon

parts.note: a teaser is a brain-teaser or puzzle
a vice is a clamp that grips work on a bench

explanation.surface: A puzzle, which should be gripping, being set for the afternoon.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue plays on 'gripping': a teaser should be gripping, and a vice grips.
explanation.definitionFit: A tea service is the matching crockery set used for afternoon tea.

clue.text: Good compiler's restricted by relative increase

indicators.note: restricted by means hemmed in, so the relative surrounds the good and the compiler

parts.note: an aunt is a relative
the compiler is the setter, who calls themself me; the 's is 'is'

explanation.surface: A setter is held back by a family member's growth.
explanation.walkthrough: 'restricted by' puts G and ME inside AUNT.
explanation.definitionFit: To augment is to make larger or add to.

clue.text: Huge bird, but it needs an incredible shot to get it!

definitions.meaning: a very large seabird with a vast wingspan

definitions.text: but it needs an incredible shot to get it!
definitions.meaning: in golf a hole played in three under par, needing remarkable strokes

explanation.definitionFit: The great seabird gives its name to golf's three-under-par score, rarer than an eagle.

clue.text: Glorious ordinal?

parts.note: the Glorious one of August, a numbered day, is the start of the British grouse-shooting season

explanation.surface: A splendid position in a sequence.
explanation.walkthrough: The Glorious Twelfth is 12 August, when grouse shooting opens in Britain.
explanation.definitionFit: The ordinal after eleventh, famous in the phrase for the grouse season's opening day.

clue.text: Expose oneself with a daffodil, perhaps? Photographer might use it

parts.note: to flash is to expose oneself indecently
a daffodil grows from a bulb; perhaps marks it as an example

explanation.surface: A flasher bares all clutching a daffodil.
explanation.definitionFit: Old cameras fired a single-use lamp to light the scene.

clue.text: Two items of underwear, so the least likely to freeze?

parts.note: a bra is an item of underwear
a vest is a British undershirt

explanation.surface: Wearing two layers of underwear keeps out the cold.
explanation.walkthrough: 'freeze' looks like cold, but means freeze with fear; a VEST is a British undershirt.
explanation.definitionFit: The most courageous are those least likely to be paralysed by fear.

clue.text: Get four or six in test that's not important

indicators.note: in places the numeral inside the test word

parts.note: a trial is a test
IV is four in Roman numerals; read the other way it is VI, six

explanation.surface: Scoring a boundary in a cricket Test match that does not matter.
explanation.walkthrough: Either works: IV after TR, or VI after TRI. In cricket a four or six is a boundary, and a Test is an international match.
explanation.definitionFit: Something trivial is of little significance.

clue.text: Bird broke away?

parts.note: bust means penniless
RD (road) is a way

explanation.surface: A bird broke free.
explanation.walkthrough: 'broke away' reads as escaped, but splits as BUST, A and RD (road, a way).
explanation.definitionFit: Bustards are large ground-dwelling birds of open country.

clue.text: Lowest titled commoner? Not quite! Thatcher's first!

annotationWithheld.why: Lowest titled commoner? Not quite! Thatcher's first!: BARONE(SS) needs 'Thatcher's' for BARONESS while 'Thatcher's first' gives T, so the one word does two jobs
annotationWithheld.clue: Lowest titled commoner? Not quite! Thatcher's first!

clue.text: Ancient garment, one understood to be the wrong way round

indicators.text: to be the wrong way round
indicators.note: the wrong way round means the letters of both pieces are read backwards

parts.note: A means one
got means understood, as in 'I got it'

explanation.surface: An old robe, which someone grasped had been put on back to front.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to be the wrong way round' turns A GOT into TOGA.
explanation.definitionFit: The Roman toga was a draped robe of classical antiquity.

clue.text: Raw chips offered up around this?

definitions.meaning: in golf, short lofted shots are played up onto the putting surface from around it

explanation.definitionFit: Green means inexperienced; in golf, chips are played onto the putting surface.

clue.text: Yesterday in France, a larch shook along the branches

parts.note: hier is French for yesterday

indicators.note: shook suggests the letters of a larch are shaken up

explanation.surface: Yesterday in France a larch tree shook along its boughs.
explanation.walkthrough: 'shook' rearranges A LARCH into ARCHAL.
explanation.definitionFit: A hierarchy branches like a tree, rank under rank, so something hierarchal runs through such branches.

clue.text: Kiss after midnight? The solution will be rubber!

indicators.note: after places the kiss letter behind the time word

parts.note: midnight is a late hour
X is a kiss at the end of a letter

explanation.surface: A late kiss leads somewhere risqué; the answer will be rubber.
explanation.walkthrough: 'after' puts X behind LATE; latex is a milky liquid from which rubber is made.
explanation.definitionFit: Latex is the milky sap of the rubber tree, and the word also means the rubber made from it.

clue.text: I must be mad!

explanation.definitionFit: The setter's pseudonym is also slang for crazy.

clue.text: Dramatic work turning into one in the theatre

parts.note: an opera is a staged musical drama

indicators.note: turning means the word into is twisted round into a new order

explanation.surface: A drama becomes a theatrical event.
explanation.walkthrough: 'theatre' is the operating theatre, not a stage; 'turning' rearranges INTO into TION.
explanation.definitionFit: Surgery is carried out in a hospital's operating theatre.

clue.text: "The Kalaallitt of Greenland"-I knew it would be pronounced wrong!

indicators.note: pronounced wrong says the phrase I knew it is spoken carelessly to give the letters entered

parts.note: the words run together when said

explanation.surface: Someone predicted that the Greenlanders' name would be mispronounced.
explanation.definitionFit: The Kalaallit are Greenland's indigenous people, part of the wider Arctic group.

clue.text: FT compilers ask for a contract, though given a hole in the head!

definitions.text: FT compilers ask for a contract, though given a hole in the head!

parts.words: FT compilers ask for a contract, though given a hole in the head!
parts.note: setters wanting a contract would say 'sign us', which sounds like a cavity in the skull

explanation.surface: Setters seek a deal despite being half-witted.
explanation.walkthrough: Asking for a contract, the setters say 'sign us'; spoken, that is a cavity in the skull's bones. 'A hole in the head' is also slang for something useless.
explanation.definitionFit: A sinus is an air-filled cavity in the bones of the skull.

clue.text: There's a hole in the front door-Spooner wants improved security

indicators.note: Reverend Spooner swapped the opening sounds of words

parts.note: better means improved
locks give security

explanation.surface: A householder wants stronger locks for the front door.
explanation.walkthrough: Swapping the opening sounds of BETTER LOCKS gives LETTER BOCKS. A letterbox here is the mail slot in a British front door.
explanation.definitionFit: A slot in a door lets the post be pushed through.
